Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

17 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: the bird's head and eye, just left of center in the upper half Light: the low sun at the upper right, so every lit edge faces up and to the rightHow this lesson was made

Get these out of the box before you start. Every paint in the lesson is mixed from them; squeeze out a little of each when its step comes up.

  • Titanium whitefirst in step 1
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)first in step 1
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)first in step 1
  • Ultramarine bluefirst in step 1
  • Burnt siennafirst in step 1

What you need

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the misty sky from lavender to goldFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Paint the pale sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: Dry-brush the far misty trunksFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff brush, about 1/2 inch: Dab the hazy rust foliageOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 3/4 inch flat: Pull the trunk and branch in bark brownFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #10 round: Block in the four leaves in red-orangeRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch filbert: Block in the body in warm goldFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • 1/2 inch filbert: Shade the belly away from the lightFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • small fan brush: Flick in the cream chest feathersFan: bristles spread like a fan, for grass, fur, and soft blending
  • #6 round: Press in the dark wing and tail feathersRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #1 liner: Line in the legs and toesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 16 x 12 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Using another size? Scale every measurement.
  • A ruler
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

All 13 paints and their recipes. Each step lists the ones it needs, so you can mix as you go

You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The misty sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 17 · The misty sky, 1 of 2

Blend the misty sky from lavender to gold

  1. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  2. Paints, from the sun outward: Warm gold around the sun at the upper right, then Misty lavender-gray toward the edges.
  3. Mix enough Warm gold for this step and steps 8 and 9; cover it between them.
  4. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: Don't put too much paint on the brush. Less paint often blends better. If the paint starts to drag, add a tiny bit of water to the brush.
  5. Work fast, in one area, while both colors are still wet.
  6. It should leave a soft transition, only where both paints were still wet.
  7. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  8. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light comes from the low sun at the upper right, so every highlight in this painting sits on the upper right of what it lights. Start with warm gold in a wide patch around where the sun will go, about 4 1/2 in from the right edge, then work the lavender-gray in from the edges and blend where they meet. Paint straight across where the branch and the bird will go.

Stroke: Wet-on-wet blend how to do it here, adapted for this painting, not checked yet

Wet-on-wet blend

Adapted for this painting from the Wet-on-wet blend card, not checked yet

The general Wet-on-wet blend card (its file)

With. flat; wash brush

Load. Don't put too much paint on the brush. Less paint often blends better. If the paint starts to drag, add a tiny bit of water to the brush.

Motion. Work fast across the whole canvas while the warm gold and the lavender-gray are both still wet.

What it leaves. A soft change from gold around the sun to misty lavender-gray at the edges, only where both paints were still wet.

Then. Stop when the paint drags; streaks in the mist can stay.

Blend the gold into the lavender while both are wet

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • The sky paint turns gooey and pulls up. It has started to set. Acrylic stays wet for only a few minutes. Stop. Let it dry, then blend a new layer on top.
  • Muddy, grayish-brown sky where gold and lavender met. Overblending. Blend a few strokes and stop. Visible streaks often look natural.

STEP 2 OF 17 · The misty sky, 2 of 2

Paint the pale sun

  1. Let the misty glowing sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 4 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 1 1/2 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Pale sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #8 round.
  6. Small circles with the tip of the brush, moving outward from the middle of the sun.
  7. It should leave a soft round disc with a soft edge.
  8. Watch out: The edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter passes. Smudging with a finger works too.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Keep it small, about 1 1/2 in across, and soft at the edge so it glows rather than sits on top. Leave the gold around it.

The far woods 2 steps

STEP 3 OF 17 · The far woods, 1 of 2

Dry-brush the far misty trunks

  1. Let the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom. Its left side is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge and its right side is about 1/4 in from the right edge.
  4. Paint: Misty blue-gray.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  6. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  7. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  8. Watch out: Trunks that look solid and sharp. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the misty sky back over part of it.

Tip: Pull each trunk straight down from the top edge to the bottom, the left one a little wider. Keep them faint so the mist shows through; they're far away, so no light side and no bark.

STEP 4 OF 17 · The far woods, 2 of 2

Dab the hazy rust foliage

  1. Let the far misty trunks and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Soft rust.
  4. Mix enough Soft rust for this step and step 6; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: old stiff brush, about 1/2 inch. Load: A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.
  6. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  7. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  8. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Make them loose clumps a few inches across, as the Where picture shows: a big group on the right, some at the left edge, and some low in the middle. Keep the edges soft and broken; these are far away in the mist, so no single leaves.

Dabbing also called stippling

Adapted for this painting from the Dabbing card, not checked yet

The general Dabbing card (its file)

With. round (the tip, for small dots); old stiff brush (for rough patches); a sponge, for soft patches

Load. A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.

Motion. Tap with the tip of the brush in loose clumps. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.

What it leaves. Soft dappled clumps of far leaves that get more solid the more you tap.

Then. Keep the clumps broken at the edges so the mist shows between the taps.

The branch 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 17 · The branch, 1 of 2

Pull the trunk and branch in bark brown

  1. Let the far woods and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Bark brown.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  5. Press the full width of the brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge or tip and lighten the pressure. With an angle brush, the lighter you press, the thinner the line.
  6. It should leave a line that starts wide and tapers to a point.
  7. Watch out: Branches that look like stiff sticks. Every branch the same width and straight. Fix: start thick at the trunk and taper. Let branches fork in different directions and overlap.

Tip: Start with the trunk on the left, thick at the bottom left corner and thinner as it rises to the top. Then pull the branch from the trunk in one arch that peaks under where the bird sits and comes down to the lower right, thinning as it goes, and add the thin twigs at the right end and the small stems the leaves hang from.

STEP 6 OF 17 · The branch, 2 of 2

Catch the light on the top of the bark

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Soft rust.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 5 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Soft rust is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  9. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Keep it on the top and right edges, facing the sun; leave the bark brown along the underside of the branch and the left of the trunk. Drag along the branch, not across it.

The hanging leaves 2 steps

STEP 7 OF 17 · The hanging leaves, 1 of 2

Block in the four leaves in red-orange

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom. Its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge and its right side is about 3 1/2 in from the right edge.
  4. Paint: Leaf red-orange.
  5. Brush: #10 round.
  6. Start each leaf with one pointed oval down its middle. Then add the lobes in curved pieces on each side, smaller toward the tip.
  7. It should leave a shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Tip: There are two at the upper left (one at the top edge, one hanging below it beside the trunk) and two hanging under the branch at the lower right. Each is a pointed leaf with a few lobes, pointing down.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.

STEP 11 OF 17 · The chickadee's body, 3 of 5

Flick in the cream chest feathers

  1. Let the chickadee and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 3/4 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 2 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 7 in wide and 5 1/2 in tall.
  3. Paint: Cream.
  4. Brush: small fan brush. Load: A light load. Too much paint makes flat blobs.
  5. A quick stroke upward from the base, lifting off as it goes, so each mark thins at the top.
  6. It should leave tapered marks with broken tips, denser at the base.
  7. Leave what steps 9 and 10 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: The feathers turn into a flat smooth patch. Too much paint on the brush, or the strokes are blended together.
  9. Fix: wipe the brush nearly dry, make each flick short and separate, and let it dry before adding more.

Tip: Flick down and out along the round of the chest, most of them on the upper right where the light hits, and a few short ones along the back of the head on the right. Add a few short flicks low on the body under the wing. Leave the buff shadow and some warm gold showing low on the belly.

STEP 16 OF 17 · The feet, 1 of 2

Line in the legs and toes

  1. Let the chickadee's body and the branch dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 2 1/2 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall.
  5. Paint: Soft black.
  6. Brush: #1 liner. Load: Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.
  7. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull each leg down from the belly, then curl the short toes over the branch.
  8. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  9. Watch out: Lines that feather or spread. Laid into a wet layer underneath. Fix: let the area underneath dry first.

Tip: Two short legs come down from the belly, about 1 in apart, and the toes curl over the top of the branch.

Before starting

Subject: A black-capped chickadee on a curved bare branch with four orange and gold autumn leaves hanging from it, in front of a misty autumn wood with a low sun at the upper right.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: The image is a painted scene filling the frame edge to edge: no bars, borders, text, or watermark.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: about 0.6 in of misty background from each side (11% of the photo's width)

Why: No canvas was named, so fit-canvas picked the standard size closest to the photo's 3:2 shape (12x16, landscape). A crop keeps the bird, the whole branch curve, and every hanging leaf.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: none. Textures of hundreds of items: none (busy measured 0.7%; the background foliage is already a few soft masses of dabs). Detail inside big shapes: none beyond one repeated mark (feathers are soft flicks, bark is dry-brush). Parts: about eight at this canvas size, within the budget of 8 (16x12 is 192 sq in, so the budget stays as is).

Changed: none

Why: The source is already a loose painting a beginner could follow; a beginner render would only drift the subject.

Fine texture measured: the photo 0.7% of the canvas

A small round bird is the whole point: a black cap and bib, a white cheek, a buff chest lit from the upper right, on a curving bark branch, in front of a misty gold-and-lavender wood. The hard parts are keeping the background soft and far away and placing the bird's head pattern; the lesson is about building the bird from simple shapes over a background painted straight through.

Subject: A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch
Focal point: the bird's head and eye, just left of center in the upper half
Light: the low sun at the upper right, so every lit edge faces up and to the right

What it saw, back to front

  1. Misty glowing sky
  2. The branch
  3. The four hanging leaves
  4. The chickadee
  5. Legs and feet
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front, fits a soft misty background with one subject in front, and it's the only technique with version 2 keys.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It has no version 2 keys, so the v2 pipeline can't plan with it; the owner also picked paint-along for acrylic beginners.

How the paint recipes were worked out13 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

    Mixer: 8 parts white, 3 parts ultramarine, 3 parts burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

  • Warm gold Delta E 2.0
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 1 part yellow, 1 part red, 1 part burnt sienna

  • Pale sun yellow Delta E 1.7
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 8 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red

  • Misty blue-gray Delta E 2.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part ultramarine, 1 part white, a touch of yellow, a touch of red

  • Soft rust Delta E 3.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white, a touch of red

  • Bark brown Delta E 1.3

  • Leaf red-orange Delta E 2.0

Furthest off: Delta E 5.7. Real tubes vary by brand, so mix, compare with the step picture, and nudge.

Why the steps go in this order17 steps

Back to front: the sky blended wet first and run under everything, then the sun, the far trunks and the hazy foliage on the dry sky, then the branch painted over the background, the leaves hanging from it, the bird's body, wing, head and cheek, and the feet last because they curl over the branch.

  1. 1. Blend the misty sky from lavender to gold

    The farthest thing and the whole canvas: one wet blend from the gold glow to the lavender mist, painted straight through where everything else goes.

  2. 2. Paint the pale sun

    The sun sits in the sky, so it goes on the dry sky before anything in front of it.

  3. 3. Dry-brush the far misty trunks

    The far trunks are the next layer back in the mist, dry-brushed so they stay soft.

  4. 4. Dab the hazy rust foliage

    The hazy foliage hangs in front of the far trunks, one dab pass at this distance.

  5. 5. Pull the trunk and branch in bark brown

    The branch is in front of the whole background, so it goes on once that's dry, dark first.

  6. 6. Catch the light on the top of the bark

    The light on the bark comes after its dark coat, on the side facing the sun.

  7. 7. Block in the four leaves in red-orange

    The leaves hang from the branch, so they go on after it, as one red-orange block-in.

  8. 8. Light the gold leaves and the sunny sides

    Two leaves turn gold and the red ones get their sunny edges once the block-in is dry.

  9. 9. Block in the body in warm gold

    The bird is nearest after the branch: its whole shape first, in its middle value.

  10. 10. Shade the belly away from the light

    The darker belly patch goes on the dry block-in before the light feathers, darkest first.

  11. 11. Flick in the cream chest feathers

    The cream feathers are the light on the chest, after the shade.

  12. 12. Block in the wing and tail in gray

    The wing lies over the body, so it comes after the body is done.

  13. 13. Press in the dark wing and tail feathers

    The dark feathers go on the dry gray wing.

  14. 14. Paint the black cap and bib

    The cap and bib sit on the head the block-in already made; the strongest dark goes near the end.

  15. 15. Paint the white cheek

    The white cheek sits between the cap and bib, so it goes after them.

  16. 16. Line in the legs and toes

    The feet curl over the branch and the body, so they're last.

  17. 17. Catch the light on the toes

    The light on the toes is the final detail.

Filters it tried6 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams4 steps, free

A beginner can start every step from its picture and words; the four shaped block-ins (the leaves, the bird's body, the wing and tail, and the cap and bib) need a diagram for how to build the shape.

  • Step 7: Block in the four leaves in red-orange beginner check

    Noticed: Four lobed leaves appear whole in one step.

    Pieces: A pointed middle oval, then a lobe each side, then smaller lobes lower down, as maple-like leaves are drawn.

  • Step 9: Block in the body in warm gold beginner check

    Noticed: The whole bird appears in one step as a shaped object.

    Pieces: A round body oval, the head circle on its upper right, then the tail wedge to the lower left.

  • Step 12: Block in the wing and tail in gray beginner check

    Noticed: Where the wing sits on the body isn't clear from words alone.

    Pieces: A long oval along the back from under the head, then the narrow tail continuing it.

  • Step 14: Paint the black cap and bib beginner check

    Noticed: The cap and bib are two dark pieces with the cheek's gap between them.

    Pieces: The cap over the top of the head first, then the bib under the beak, leaving the gap for the cheek.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A wet blend over the whole canvas: the picture and the color order are enough.
  • Step 2: A small round disc; the words say how.
  • Step 3: Two straight vertical strokes.
  • Step 4: One repeated dab mark; the Where picture shows the clumps.
  • Step 5: The branch's shape is in the picture and the thick-to-thin card shows the stroke.
  • Step 6: A dry-brush pass along the top of the branch.
  • Step 8: Gold on the existing leaf shapes.
  • Step 10: One small patch, placed in the tip.
  • Step 11: One repeated flick; the card's diagram shows it.
  • Step 13: Repeated press-and-lift strokes along the wing.
  • Step 15: One small curved band between shapes already painted.
  • Step 16: Two short lines with toes; the card and the tip cover it.
  • Step 17: One short line per toe.
What the reviewer caught6 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check The first finish turned the misty lavender-gray background into a saturated bright blue and brightened the far foliage; redone once with the photo, which fixed both.
  • Text check: vague Step 1: The paints line said 'top to bottom', but the gold sits around the sun at the upper right and the lavender-gray at the edges (x 0-100, y 0-100). (fixed)
  • Text check: missing Step 5: The flat coat shows small round knobs at the ends of the two leaf stems (x 13, y 13; x 67, y 80), the tops of the leaves the branch's outline took. (left: covered by the leaves in step 7)
  • Text check: missing Step 8: The red leaves get darker red veins and patches (x 12-20, y 13-20; x 66-75, y 79-84) that no paint in this step names. (left: small, and the leaves read right without it)
  • Text check: wrong_result Step 10: The tip put the shade on the lower left under the wing; the picture shows one patch at the bottom middle of the belly (x 40-51, y 46-56). (fixed)
  • Text check: missing Step 11: Cream also appears along the back of the head (x 52-56, y 15-22) and a few streaks low on the body (x 33-46, y 42-52); the tip only named the chest. (fixed)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The first finish render pushed the misty lavender-gray background to a saturated blue; one redo passing the photo fixed it.
  • The foliage outline first took the lavender mist patches as foliage (37% of it was #9e9ba9); giving colors_out with the measured mist colors and replacing two points_in that landed on mist and glow fixed it in one round.
  • The bird's shade pass first pointed at the misty lavender-gray (merged into the bird by paints) and painted almost nothing; paints --add bird gave a buff shadow that matches the belly.
  • No Agent tool in this session, so the fresh-context text review was done in the same context (review_context: same).

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.

  • Step 5, Pull the trunk and branch in bark brown: The flat coat shows small round knobs at the ends of the two leaf stems (x 13, y 13; x 67, y 80), the tops of the leaves the branch's outline took.
  • Step 8, Light the gold leaves and the sunny sides: The red leaves get darker red veins and patches (x 12-20, y 13-20; x 66-75, y 79-84) that no paint in this step names.
  • The text review was done by the same session that wrote the text, not a fresh one.
